latest_post.title: David Walliams goes off-Brand, Libraries Commons is launched, Shropshire cuts, and an AI corruption case in India
latest_post.author: Ian Anstice / The Library Campaign

editorial.text: Leaving aside the horribleness of the David Walliams case for those involved, it’s been interesting to see how public libraries have dealt with it. Their response has largely been to wait for a national statement from Libraries Connected before doing anything. Purely from publicly available sources (and I know of many more privately), I count 34 services who have kept the disgraced author’s books on their shelves, and just 2 who have taken them off. Somewhat worryingly, it’s been the Far Right who have been the ones most vocal in agreeing with this strategy, with Unherd and Restore being in favour (perhaps showing the truth of the old adage that a stopped clock is correct twice a day) but, apart from this, it’s been great to see library services doing something en bloc together rather than going their own way. I have difficulty thinking this would have been the case twenty years ago and is a tribute to the respect that Libraries Connected has garnered since it was set up that it happened this week. Perhaps herding cats is not impossible, at least some of the time. What would have been the big news this week – Shropshire library cuts and the launch of Library Commons – has to take second place. Shropshire has announced what looks like a quite severe cost-cutting move – it could close two libraries and its mobile, plus cut the hours of six main libraries. One suspects that there will be the usual campaign groups, consultation (possibly even genuine), the attempted volunteerisation of opposition etc in future months so watch out for that. In more positive news, there’s been the launch of a website dedicated to public library data. Well done, as ever, to Libraries Hacked for trying to get something sorted. This is especially important after the largely unexpected loss of LibraryOn but, frankly, has been needed for decades. Considering its stock in trade, it’s always been embarrassing that the public libraries sector has been so rubbish in publishing information about itself and I hope this can change. My thanks to Dave Rowe, the force behind Libraries Hacked, for answering some questions about it below. Finally, public libraries have made big news in India in the last week or two as a massive corruption case has come to light with due to a new library having lots of fake books in it. Fake, that is, because they appear to be AI-written knock-offs. Over seventy thousand books have had to be withdrawn, with five library staff suspended, and the crisis becoming a major political football. This is the first time I’ve seen something like this. Mind you, it’s also been the first time that I’ve seen a library mural with a three-winged parrot included. Yet another AI problem to consider I guess. Whoopee doo. editorial.html:
Leaving aside the horribleness of the David Walliams case for those involved, it’s been interesting to see how public libraries have dealt with it. Their response has largely been to wait for a national statement from Libraries Connected before doing anything. Purely from publicly available sources (and I know of many more privately), I count 34 services who have kept the disgraced author’s books on their shelves, and just 2 who have taken them off. Somewhat worryingly, it’s been the Far Right who have been the ones most vocal in agreeing with this strategy, with Unherd and Restore being in favour (perhaps showing the truth of the old adage that a stopped clock is correct twice a day) but, apart from this, it’s been great to see library services doing something en bloc together rather than going their own way. I have difficulty thinking this would have been the case twenty years ago and is a tribute to the respect that Libraries Connected has garnered since it was set up that it happened this week. Perhaps herding cats is not impossible, at least some of the time.

What would have been the big news this week – Shropshire library cuts and the launch of Library Commons – has to take second place. Shropshire has announced what looks like a quite severe cost-cutting move – it could close two libraries and its mobile, plus cut the hours of six main libraries. One suspects that there will be the usual campaign groups, consultation (possibly even genuine), the attempted volunteerisation of opposition etc in future months so watch out for that. In more positive news, there’s been the launch of a website dedicated to public library data. Well done, as ever, to Libraries Hacked for trying to get something sorted. This is especially important after the largely unexpected loss of LibraryOn but, frankly, has been needed for decades. Considering its stock in trade, it’s always been embarrassing that the public libraries sector has been so rubbish in publishing information about itself and I hope this can change. My thanks to Dave Rowe, the force behind Libraries Hacked, for answering some questions about it below.

Finally, public libraries have made big news in India in the last week or two as a massive corruption case has come to light with due to a new library having lots of fake books in it. Fake, that is, because they appear to be AI-written knock-offs. Over seventy thousand books have had to be withdrawn, with five library staff suspended, and the crisis becoming a major political football. This is the first time I’ve seen something like this. Mind you, it’s also been the first time that I’ve seen a library mural with a three-winged parrot included. Yet another AI problem to consider I guess. Whoopee doo.

Mobile library to serve Acocks Green while library closed – Birmingham Now. “A mobile library with thousands of books will serve the community while Acocks Green Library remains closed for roof replacement.” … “Residents should expect to use the mobile library for a long period as Acocks Green Liberal Democrats said on their social media that “it will be there every Wednesday, until the Library reopens, which is likely to take just over a year”.”

stories.text: Glasgow primary school wins award after fight to save library – Glasgow Times. Paywall. “Cardonald Primary in Glasgow has won the UNICEF UK’s Gold Rights Respecting Award for its efforts to save the local library. The award recognizes schools that prioritize children’s rights and create a respectful environment for all. The school’s pupils actively campaigned for the library’s preservation, and the award is a testament to their commitment to safeguarding the library and promoting a respectful school community.”

stories.text: Osterley To Become Borough’s First Self-service Library – Brentford TW8. “Osterley is set to become the first library in the London Borough of Hounslow to introduce self-service access, with extended opening hours expected to launch in early 2027. The move forms part of Hounslow Council’s wider programme to introduce self-access technology in community hubs and libraries across the borough. Under the scheme, registered library members will be able to enter and use the library during additional unstaffed hours, supplementing the existing staffed service.” … “Plans approved for consultation would see all 11 of the borough’s community hubs and libraries equipped with self-access technology, allowing members to use facilities outside traditional opening hours. The programme is backed by a £1.2 million capital investment and is intended to significantly increase access to library buildings without substantially increasing staffing costs.”

stories.text: Cross-sector partnership helps young people shape future services and build skills for the digital economy – Sync NI. “The six-week programme combined paid work experience, emerging technologies and real-world problem solving, challenging participants to answer a live brief from Libraries NI: How might we reimagine libraries around what young people truly value? stories.text: Newton-le-Willows library move faces further council work – Warrington Guardian. “In September, the council launched an engagement exercise to seek residents’ views on the potential relocation of Newton-le-Willows Library to the newly-restored Grade II listed Earlestown Town Hall. The consultation formed part of ongoing discussions arising from the borough’s library strategy, adopted by the previous council administration in 2023.” … “While respondents expressed reservations about the proposal, the consultation clearly identified two principal areas where “further information and assurance are needed”. The most frequently raised concerns related to whether Earlestown Town Hall could accommodate the full range of existing library services, activities and resources, and what the future of the historic Carnegie library building would be should a relocation be pursued. In light of the feedback received, the council is undertaking further design and feasibility work to address the key concerns raised by residents.”

stories.text: The library: more than just a place to borrow a book – The Press. “I must admit my initial reaction to some of this was one of mild bewilderment. A library with a gaming zone? A library with a laser cutter? It turns out that the problem isn’t with modern libraries, but my rather stubborn attachment to the past. What I’d failed to appreciate is that the purpose of a library was never really the books. They were simply the best technology available for doing the job. The job is making knowledge, ideas and the tools to explore them accessible to everyone, regardless of their means.”
